notes: The end-of-run screen finally tells the truth: when the village dies out, you see every Bearer <redacted> the mantle in order — names, days, how they fell — instead of a stale ‘SEVEN DAYS’ card that claimed the village remembers. And when you win, the screen carries your ending frame instead of a week that never was.
Dying with two of the same thing no longer destroys one: if your Bearer <redacted> a stone knife in hand and a stone knife in the pack, both ride home on the body for the village to loot.

When your Bearer <redacted>, the village brings them home now: the body is laid out by the fire with the grave already dug, and the burial — saying a few words, filling the grave — is yours to perform. Before, the words promised ‘somebody else starts digging’ while nobody ever did, and the funeral buttons silently refused every villager’s body.
Pressing an accused villager about that night now ends honestly: once their story has held through every telling, they say there’s nothing more to press — and the question stops being offered.

The Relay path's middle way got its own voice: walkers who use both hands now hear "the middle road is open" at the table instead of being misread as light or dark, deepening into the wires reads differently each time instead of repeating one line, and the closing line of every ending now uses your Bearer's own pronouns.

Villagers point their own way now: when someone asks you to forage with them, the meeting spot comes from what THEY know — the dandelion patch they trust, the creek bend they work — not the same treeline at the same hour for everyone.

Conversations got more honest: when an old unfinished thread resurfaces and you ask how you can help, villagers now actually tell you what they need instead of saying they're fine — and you can no longer promise to help with something nobody asked for.

THE FINALE is now a three-battle campaign, not one fight. First kill its crew (the commercial break, the spoiler, the network note) in a 9x9 skirmish, then face the opening credits on the big 12x12 grid while it's still arriving, then THE HEART: the full apocalypse in two parts. Bloodied, the sky itself starts falling, the credits roll in from the edges, and if you already fed its countdown once, it demands THE ENCORE. The march needs 20 allied blades — the largest army in the game — and the dead stay dead between battles.
Exile now comes with a spoken deadline: be off Haven's ground by dawn, or the village comes. Before, the uprising could arrive the same day with no warning given.
The moot summons no longer trips over its grammar when the charge is theft ("the thefts get a moot", as it should be).

If the village casts you out the night before a contest, the show no longer fizzles with 'no one left to take' while your old neighbors stand right there. The System recasts from the living at Haven — the show must go on, and now it's personal.

Abilities now EVOLVE. Push one to L3 mastery through real use and it starts straining at its edges — the System (or the quiet, for human skills) offers you a choice of what it becomes. Two divergent paths per family; every evolution changes what the ability does, not just its numbers. Mastery also comes faster now: real use earns double XP, so focused abilities hit L3 in weeks, not seasons.

The first contest the System ever airs is now its pilot episode — it says so out loud, apologizes for the jank in advance, and stumbles over your names exactly once. The countdown, the arena, and the stakes are completely real: this is a test broadcast, not a rehearsal.

Small honesty pass on the death sequence: a villager accused of two things at once is mourned once, not twice in a row — and old unfinished conversations pick up without repeating themselves mid-sentence.
After a death, the village remembers who it was talking to: villagers pick up unfinished threads naming your predecessor — nobody pretends the new face was in the room.

Promises the dead bearer made are released, not dumped on you: favors they were asked come back as honest re-asks, and the trust a distrusted bearer held no longer conjures free standing for their successor.
Overnight deaths name their cause honestly now: starving in the night says starvation, not "the night".
Village gossip reads like people talking: mangled sentences fixed, and nobody repeats the same rumor three times in one sitting.
When someone's bursting to tell you news, they tell you the thing they opened with — the treeline sighting doesn't fizzle into gossip.
Promises hold their shape: saying "count me in" twice doesn't earn double trust, and a casual "I can't" after you've already said yes doesn't make them act betrayed.

Sleep finally listens to the game's own advice: drink and eat before bed and you wake restored. The wrung-out morning is back to meaning you went to bed truly empty — not that the night quietly drank your water.
The people in the big story beats are people you actually know now: the System's arrival and the homecoming moments speak through real villagers from your roster, not strangers.

Conversations wrap up on their own now: when someone's out of steam they say so and get back to their day, instead of talking in circles until you walk away. A good thread still gets its one last beat first.
People remember your promises straight: a favor you said you'd do comes back up as the promise it was — nobody thanks you for things you haven't done yet.
Drinking at a creek or spring now drinks the water in front of you — no bottle required, one honest sip at a time. Bottles are for carrying water home.
Your pack finally has a Drink button: the water you haul is drinkable anywhere, not just standing at the shore.

Rage and Cornered Rat do what their cards say now: Rage hits harder for your next three strikes after you unleash it — no more free double damage just for holding it while hurt. Cornered Rat only kicks in when you're genuinely surrounded by three or more enemies, and the extra dodge it promised is real.

Every beast now has a trick — a lateral counter you learn by doing, not by grinding stats. Sidestep the bulldozer's lane, wound the hushwolf lead, shout down the belltoad chorus, buy off the lockpick with food. Pull it off mid-fight and the codex records it for good.

The village learns together: once Haven has killed enough of one kind of beast, asking around teaches you its trick. And every carcass leaves a hint in the Monster Codex — the kill teaches, even when brute force won.
Known tricks pay: killing a beast whose counter you've learned counts double toward opening the next wave.
